messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Vignette:
Mr. Johnson is a 77-year-old African-American man who has been married for over five decades and currently serves as a school principal in his local community. Mr. Johnson experienced a traumatic event approximately six months ago when he was assaulted by an intruder at the school where he works. The incident occurred late one afternoon after most students had left, but a few were still on campus. An intoxicated individual broke into the building and forcibly entered Mr. Johnson’s office, demanding money. The traumatic experience left profound imprints on his daily life. He now experiences intense distress whenever he encounters smells reminiscent of alcohol. The assault involved being forced to do things against his will, leaving him with a deep-seated fear of losing control or autonomy. This has translated into frequent scanning of exits as soon as he enters any room or building, and an exaggerated startle response to sudden movements around him. The memory of the event is complex and laden with grief. Each time Mr. Johnson remembers what happened, he feels an overwhelming sense of loss and sorrow. Auditory flashbacks are common; often, he hears snippets of sounds from that day—shouting or breaking glass—as if they were still happening in his head. Sometimes, these memories feel so detached that he almost feels numb, as though the event happened to someone else. Mr. Johnson has come to believe that he cannot rely on himself during such moments, which exacerbates his sense of vulnerability. He frequently blames himself for the assault, believing that if he had acted differently or been more cautious, the incident might have been avoided. This self-blame is compounded by a growing mistrust in others; he finds it difficult to trust even close colleagues and friends. These symptoms began manifesting immediately following the assault but grew worse over time. At work, Mr. Johnson’s scanning behavior has made him appear distracted or preoccupied, leading to misunderstandings with his staff. He often avoids social gatherings where alcohol is served or where there might be a crowd, which has strained his relationships with colleagues and friends. The cumulative impact of these symptoms has taken its toll on both his personal and professional life. His marriage has been affected by the isolation he seeks in order to avoid triggers; he withdraws emotionally from his wife, leaving her feeling unsupported and confused about what’s happening. Mr. Johnson finally decided to seek help after a particularly distressing episode at work where an unexpected noise caused him to react so severely that it alarmed those around him. He realized that the fear of another incident and the persistent feelings of grief were overwhelming and affecting his ability to function effectively in both his personal and professional life. What frightens Mr. Johnson most is the prospect of never feeling safe again, of always being on edge, and of not being able to trust himself or others in crucial moments. Despite these fears, he is hopeful that with help, he might be able to regain a sense of control over his life and find ways to cope with the memories and triggers without them dominating his daily existence. He seeks support to navigate through this difficult time and reclaim a sense of normalcy and trust in both himself and others around him.
